endorsements.quote: Community-led governance bodies with real decision-making power over technology choices.
Iterative co-design that prioritizes Indigenous design principles.
Every data collection effort must produce concrete, community-defined benefits that flow back to the source.

The implication for digital health and AI is blunt: any screening or risk-stratification algorithm calibrated on urban non-Indigenous data, deployed without local recalibration and community-controlled validation, will misclassify Indigenous health in ways that look statistically clean but are clinically wrong [2, 10].

unlisted_practices: Obtain free, prior and informed consent (FPIC) from Indigenous communities before deploying AI applications or digital health tools, especially those handling territorial health data or Indigenous knowledge.
Place Indigenous communities in authority over collection, storage, interpretation and reuse of data about them, following CARE, OCAP and cognitive sovereignty principles.
Give community councils authority over whether a digital platform is adopted, how it is modified, and when it is shut down.
Design AI and automation to support human healers, biomedical and traditional, rather than replace them.
Pass algorithmic outputs to Indigenous knowledge holders for interpretation rather than treating them as recommendations in their own right.
Partially or fully community-own AI systems trained on Indigenous health data, with benefit-sharing agreements covering intellectual property and commercial applications.
Include exit strategies such as clauses allowing communities to stop using a system without losing care continuity, data portability, and a defined timeline for vendor disengagement.
Evaluate digital health and AI against community-defined well-being metrics rather than vendor-defined KPIs.
Build technical capacity within Indigenous communities so their technical competence grows.
Prioritize cultural specificity over scalability in design, including language-appropriate interfaces such as Yathê when consent is given.
Maintain community capacity to function fully without digital systems and use technology only when it clearly improves outcomes without creating dependency.
Use privacy-preserving architectures such as federated learning, differential privacy and homomorphic encryption so data stays within the source community.
Integrate Indigenous observational knowledge as validated input into predictive systems.
Evaluate digital health interventions against their probable impact on the cultural-ecological substrate that protects health, not only biomedical endpoints.
Require AI and digital documentation tools to engage Indigenous knowledge at the level of species, preparation, dosage and ritual context rather than generic lookups.
Amend AI legislation to name Indigenous data sovereignty and require FPIC for AI applications drawing on Indigenous knowledge.

screen.reason: The paper provides an ethical and epistemological governance framework (the Ancestral-Digital Ethnomedicine Framework) based on a scoping review and regional data synthesis for deploying digital health and AI in Indigenous communities.
